content: Telemedicine refers to the use of electronic communication technologies to deliver healthcare services to patients when there is a physical distance between the healthcare provider and the patient. In the context of neonatal intensive care units (NICUs), where newborn infants often require specialized and intensive medical care, parents and families need substantial support from healthcare professionals, both in terms of information and time. Telemedicine has the potential to enhance this support by bridging the gap created by physical separation. The objective of this study was to determine whether telemedicine technology, when used to support families of newborns receiving intensive care, has an impact on the length of the infant's hospital stay and on parental or family satisfaction with the care provided. To address this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to September 2011. Additional searches were performed on ClinicalTrials.gov and the EudraCT database, as well as in the proceedings of relevant conferences such as those of the Canadian Society of Telehealth, the American Telemedicine Association, and the International Society for Telemedicine. The selection criteria focused on identifying randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated telemedicine interventions specifically designed to support parents of infants in the NICU. These interventions were compared to standard support measures. The primary outcome of interest was the length of the infant's hospital stay, while secondary outcomes included parental and staff satisfaction, emergency hospital visits after discharge, and the family's use of infant health-related resources. Two independent reviewers screened the studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias in the included study using the standard methodology of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. Treatment effects were planned to be expressed using statistical measures such as risk ratio (RR), risk difference (RD), number needed to treat (NNT), and mean difference (MD), with a fixed-effect model applied where appropriate. Only one study met the inclusion criteria for this review. This study evaluated the use of a telemedicine program called Baby Carelink for parents and families of infants in the NICU. The intervention group, which had access to the telemedicine program, was compared to a control group that did not have access to this program. The primary outcome, the length of hospital stay, showed no significant difference between the two groups. The average length of stay for the telemedicine group was 68.5 days (standard deviation [SD] 28.3 days), while the control group had an average stay of 70.6 days (SD 35.6 days). The mean difference (MD) was -2.10 days, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from -18.85 to 14.65 days. This indicates that the use of telemedicine did not significantly reduce the length of hospital stay. Furthermore, there was insufficient data to perform a detailed analysis of family satisfaction with the care provided. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence to either support or refute the use of telemedicine technology as a means of supporting parents of high-risk newborns in the NICU. Additional clinical trials are necessary to evaluate the effectiveness of telemedicine in this context, with a focus on outcomes such as the length of hospital stay and parental perceptions of NICU care.
